title: Stepper motors
about: Motors that move in tiny exact steps, like the ones in 3D printers.

html: A stepper motor turns in tiny, exact steps.
Around the middle are coils of wire. The controller turns them on one after another, and each switch pulls the magnet in the middle around by one step.
Most steppers take 200 steps to go all the way around. That's 1.8° per step. Need a quarter turn? Send 50 steps.
3D printers, laser cutters and CNC machines use steppers to move to exact spots.
A stepper has no sensor. The controller counts the steps it sends and assumes the motor followed. That's called an open loop.
If the load is too heavy or the steps come too fast, the motor can't keep up and skips steps. The controller still thinks it's in the right place, but it isn't.
When it's stopped, a stepper holds its position strongly. That's called holding torque.

Before every print, a 3D printer homes: it moves each motor until a part taps a small switch at the edge. That switch is a touch sensor, and it tells the printer exactly where zero is. Then it counts steps from there.
If a print suddenly looks shifted halfway up, the motors probably skipped steps.

steps.q: A stepper takes 200 steps per turn. How many steps make a quarter turn?
Why can a stepper end up in the wrong place without knowing?
options: It has no sensor, so skipped steps go unnoticed
steps.explain: The controller only counts the steps it sent. If the motor skips some, nothing tells it.

steps.q: Which machine is famous for using stepper motors?
steps.explain: 3D printers move the nozzle to exact spots by counting steps.
